description: Kingdom of Poland (960–1795) beginning with Piast conversion to Christianity under Mieszko I; Casimir III's legal and urban reforms made Poland the most tolerant state in medieval Europe for Jewish refugees expelled from western kingdoms; union with Lithuania created the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth (1569), one of Europe's largest states, whose elected monarchy and noble liberum veto ultimately produced political paralysis enabling late eighteenth-century partition by neighbours.

temporal.notes: Stub: dates from GeoJSON basemap years 1000–1300

lifecycle_phases.description: Mieszko I converts to Christianity; Bolesław I Chrobry crowned king (1025); early Piast state controls lower Vistula and Oder
Kingdom divided among Piast princes; German colonisation (Ostsiedlung) introduces urban and agricultural technology; Mongol invasion (1241) devastates Kraków
Władysław I Łokietek reunites kingdom; Casimir III 'the Great' codifies law, builds 50 castles, opens Poland to Jewish refugees
Jagiellonian union with Lithuania (1386) creates largest European state; Grunwald (1410) defeats Teutonic Order; Kraków becomes Renaissance cultural centre

rise_factors.description: Casimir III's legal codifications, Statutes of Wiślica and Piotrków, created uniform law replacing regional customs and attracted skilled Jewish, German, and Armenian settlers
Jagiellonian union with Lithuania created strategic depth against Teutonic Order pressure and German imperial ambition simultaneously

decline_factors.description: Noble szlachta's liberum veto and elective monarchy created structural inability to reform governance against external threats
